>To respond to your first point about the ex-KBG bad guys in action films, I would argue that the repeated exploitation of an American audience’s general culture of fear towards Russia to make evil characters more detestable does actually say something quite interesting about the fear of the “other” and how audiences react when facing foreign cultures.

I think that point is a little too broad, in the sense that it applies to Russians specifically, who had a long Cold War with the U.S. and have, therefore, built a long tradition as "bad guys" in U.S. propaganda (which, naturally, extends to films). If you made a movie like that now but it was about a group of Danes, I think people would mostly be confused rather than be like "Well, never visiting Denmark, that's for sure".

Stereotyping exists, yes, but it can be useful for a story, both in its construction and themes, vibe, etc. and I'd say you can't apply a broad sheet to it, you have to go case by case. 

For instance, personally, I love the "Evil, Indestructible Russian" stereotype cause it's fun and I don't think any less of Russian people for it. Seriously, I love it when an action movie has a pasty, blonde, muscled dude getting beaten, stabbed, shot and run over, and still getting up again and again. Pour some vodka on those wounds, that'll heal over quick.

As for your second point, that's a very interesting way to see things, because I come from an identical background, but I have the opposite view. Growing up and (still) living in a small town with people of very limited interests, I've found a majority of people to be quite a bit uninteresting, even in the couple of colleges I've gone to.

People CAN be fascinating and a lot of them have been, but I have 0 interest in reading about regular people doing regular people things, I'd much rather read about something totally out there to experience that spark of strangeness. 

The absurdity just has more to do with accepting that the world is forever imperfect, that there are bad things and that we can't just snap our fingers and fix them from one moment to the next. I can't do much to change it all... but I can at least make fun of it and laugh in its face.

testo:
I think there’s a pretty profound difference between manufacturing drama and involving us in someone’s interior life - sometimes dramatics can be the best way to externalize that, but it can come from errant details, performance, dialogue, really anything. I think there are a couple fleeting moments where Past Lives is really good at this, namely the bar scene, which is when it blossoms and comes to life.

An emotionally resonant narrative happening in the mundane quotidian of life itself is a great tradition of cinema - from Eric Rohmer to Hong Sangsoo to Mira Nair, there is an entire spectrum of film that lets drama slowly and subtly emerge from an interior life. What the films of those artists share that Past Lives lacks (imo) is the specificity that makes a constructed world a *life* rather than a set of circumstances. Past Lives could have been a great, great film in my eyes if I saw that life, if there were observations I could make independent of what I’m being told.

testo:
I always like to watch David Lynch’s work as if I’m viewing the work of an artist in a gallery. I think his work is incredibly personal and draws on his own tastes, memories and experiences of the world. 

I’m sure you are aware of his process in which he uses transcendental meditation to “fish” for ideas in an ocean of knowledge. He says, “Down deep, the fish are more powerful and more pure.They’re huge and abstract. And they’re very beautiful.”

These ideas are always going to be informed by his personal history. My personal reading of Blue velvet is that it evokes these ideas in powerful or abstract ways. 

From memory he talks about growing up in a pretty average and pleasant American town, smiling milk man and all. When he discovered painting and art school he was exposed to another side of America. I don’t remember the timeline but he studied in Philadelphia for a time and describes the impression it left on him: “The fear, insanity, corruption, filth, despair, violence in the air was so beautiful to me,” Lynch told reporters. “It gave me a lot of ideas… and a certain way of seeing things.”

I think what you have researched so far and what others have explained is all true of the film. They all co-exist because I don’t think he is interested in one meaning or making a judgement. I think abstraction is what he is attracted to, which allows for a multitude of readings. 

So for all the overarching themes, I do actually think he is drawing from specific life experiences and the observations his makes about the world. They are reflective of his process and inner world. It’s why there is no other film maker like him.

testo:
I think we should bring Stanley Kubrick's own words into this conversation. From a contemporary interview, answering a question about why the character of Alex fascinates audiences:

>I think that it’s probably because we can identify with Alex on the unconscious level. The psychiatrists tell us the unconscious has no conscience — and perhaps in our unconscious we are all potential Alexes. It may be that only as a result of morality, the law and sometimes our own innate character that we do not become like him. Perhaps this makes some people feel uncomfortable and partly explains some of the controversy which has arisen over the film. Perhaps they are unable to accept this view of human nature. But I think you find much the same psychological phenomena at work in Shakespeare’s *Richard III.* You should feel nothing but dislike towards Richard, and yet when the role is well played, with a bit of humour and charm, you find yourself gradually making a similar kind of identification with him.

Malcolm McDowell has also compared the character to Richard III in [interviews;](https://www.theguardian.com/film/2019/apr/02/how-we-made-a-clockwork-orange-malcolm-mcdowell-stanley-kubrick) both characters are superficial charmers ultimately about appeasing their own base desires. As Kubrick notes, that is a disturbing aspect of both works -- the possibility that our fascination and even identification with these characters says something about our own dark desires.

But I don't really understand this characterization of it as pathetic.

Maybe I experience sexuality very differently than you or the average person but his reflection on that specific fantasy as presented in the film feels empathetic rather than fetishizing. Are you saying it's pathetic because of his inability to live up to his reflections on it? Also, the second repetition did not remotely make me think he wants to be ravished by a hunky naval officer, nor did any of the other repetitions. I can see how that would be a reading of it, but to me that's a reading of the film as a film rather than a world, and I think that's a childish way to watch great movies. To me, every encounter he has in the world is an attempt to square a personal, existential quest for truth and reality and, in a sense, immortality (I can fuck every woman forever, my sexuality is an endlessly unraveling relationship with the world) with a social existence that constantly reminds you your existential quest is vain and hopeless, or at least fleeting and shared with every other person - far too many to share a quest with.

Nicole's character's fantasy and the way she presents it is a coincidence of so many factors - a fight for truth, reality and mutual respect in a relationship which can instead become a fight for power, the way that fight for power is gendered, the way it's violent - you can tell from how she approaches that whole conversation that she knows that story / fantasy will translate a specific, fetishized way in Bill's head, and that she herself feels like a victim of that form of fetishization, unsure of how her sexuality exists outside of it. She also feels like she victimizes Bill through her awareness of and participation in these public sexual spectacles, their sex is performative but maybe not for each other. The entire movie feels to me like it takes place in the moments directly after she relates this fantasy to him, she makes him aware of the eyes of the entire species on their sex, something which, as a man, feeling himself territorial, private, invulnerable, he has felt he cannot afford to reflect on. The ending affirms their ability to fuck in their own room for only each other as the saving grace, the confirmation of an existence beyond the social and political. 

But again, I don't like that every time we're shown the sailor fantasy, it's Tom Cruise thinking, then the fantasy, then back to Tom thinking! I just keep thinking it would be stronger if the fantasy found its way back in moments where it's burning through the world, transitioning us from one scene to another. I just sort of don't believe he would be specifically thinking about that fantasy, because we're shown purposefully that he's being motivated by thought processes independent of that - he's shown to be thinking about the fantasy, then shown to have rather been dwelling on something else completely unrelated by what he does moments later. Do you think that's an intentional choice - to make us THINK Bill is fantasizing about Alice being fucked while he's clearly not? It feels like it's forcing us to consider that Bill is being motivated by this fantasy Alice shared even though it's already so obvious everything he does in the movie is motivated by the fantasy!

My personal theory to this is similar to my theory to getting into different music. 

Say a band is recommended to you by a lot of people who’ve clued you into other stuff you like. Whenever you try to listen to the band though you can’t get into them. Maybe years later or maybe just through one song, you find your door into the band’s music. It functions like a master key and slowly unlocks all these doors that were previously closed.

Movies, due to being regularly 30 to 40 times longer, aren’t going to give you as many times for those moments. But I would say instead of reacting to something you aren’t connecting with by saying “I don’t like that”, as most people do, think “I don’t like that right now”.

I personally have gotten very good at sussing out the difference between things I can’t connect with now but probably will at some other time. It’s not a science but it makes for a more open mind to meet the world with

>As a lover of sci-fi and Andrei Tarkovsky's Mirror (1975) I was underwhelmed. I understood its themes of humanity's profound mysteries being internal, rather than external, but man did I struggling to get through this. It's definitely beautiful but its cryptic plot and monotone dialogue almost put me to sleep.

No, apparently you appreciated very little of what Tarkovsky offered in Solaris.  Its plot is not cryptic but simple.  Further, and perhaps strangely, Tarkovsky is on record that he dislikes science fiction, and that he does not make science fiction movies (re: Stalker, Solaris):

>QUESTION. Apparently, you have always been interested in the problems of scientific and technological revolution? You are one of the few directors who make science fiction films... A. >TAPKOVSKY. You are wrong. First, many people work in this genre. Secondly, you judge me as a director of science fiction films, apparently, by Solaris. If you've watched Stalker carefully, you wouldn't say that--I hope you don't get the impression that it's a sci-fi movie. In any case, we have done everything in our power to exterminate the signs of this genre in the picture. If we talk about Solaris, I think that the main drawback of this work lies precisely in the fact that the presence of genre features and peculiarities is too noticeable in it. I have to say that I am not a fan of science fiction at all. Rather the opposite... (Andrei Tarkovsky answers questions from students of Moscow State Technical University 1981)

And:

>I was no more interested, therefore, in the fantastic plot of Stalker than I had been in the story-line of Solaris. Unfortunately the science fiction element in Solaris was nonetheless too prominent and became a distraction. The rockets and space stations--required by Lem's novel--were interesting to construct; but it seems to me now that the idea of the film would have stood out more vividly and boldly had we managed to dispense with these things altogether (Sculpting in Time p.199).

Op,
What you need here is confidence in your own tastes.  I’ve been down this road myself, and had a lot of insecurities I’ve worked through, so I won’t say this is an easy thing to do. For some people it might never be an issue, but if you’ve experienced this kind of insecurity, it can be a lot of work to overcome.

Ask yourself that without judgement, but with curiosity, what’s going on for you that makes you question yourself?


In regard to film specifically, or any art form, or really anything, just remember you have every right to like anything or dislike anything, no matter how much your opinion agrees or disagrees with other’s views of the specific in question.  

For me personally, I like any art that connects me with an emotion, or that makes me think, or that I can’t get out of my head.   The greater the intensity of those connections, the more I enjoy the piece.  But that’s just my own barometer for what I enjoy.   There are no wrong answers here, as long as the answer comes internally from you.

I highly suggest it! You have to look at it through a psychological lens and pay attention to the character arcs, dialogue, actions, and narrative structure. The details are in the world views of the characters, their own struggles, and how things are mirrored (beginning and end, normally). Nolan is a master at this, for example.

You have to think about it in terms of archetypes and relationships and dyads. Look at Robin and his orphaned state, mirroring that of Batman, placing Batman in a fatherly role. Some things you might not understand, but are deep to human nature. For example, studies show that most of the best artists lost a parent before the age of 10. So, the joke is... if you want to be a good artist, just lose a parent before your 10th birthday. It makes sense if you just think about it: that kind of pain and loss, and how it drives them forward. This is why there is another joke: every superhero is an orphan.

However, another great one is that many have two sets of parents: one earthly, the other heavenly. How did Superman get taken seriously as fiction in the 1970s? With very wise writers and school teachers going to the headmaster or whatsoever and telling him, 'Superman's story is Biblical and deeply moral'. The guy that helped create *Batman (1989)* literally tells this story in the 'making of' section, by the way.

Superman has his divine parents and the Kents, his earthly parents. Batman has his divine parents (i.e. his father, pretty much the most powerful man in Gotham) and his earthly parents (Alfred). The same is true for Harry Potter, of course. When were Frodo's parents killed? When he was 12. Not far off! Who was his earthly parent? Bilbo. (It's actually implied that Frodo comes from a fairly major family/bloodline.) You see it time and time again.

There are many themes and threads like this, you just have to learn to find and understand them, across different stories/films, etc. Then, you can spot them whenever they pop up, and make the connection right away.

I've already started to offer a commentary on *Field of Dreams (1989)*, for example, going through every major still/scene in the film. I also already did this for a YouTube video with LOTR (Fellowship of the Ring). And, I've done it in the past for the beginning of *The Dark Knight (2008)* and in general. But, you also see such things in *Finding Nemo (2004)* or all things. For example, when he's in the fish tank and must go through an initiation ritual to, in essence, 'become a man'. This is the portal between worlds. Symbolically (sometimes literally), the female form, with the male (sometimes female) hero having to pass through it. You see it in *The Little Mermaid (1989)*, and *The Lion King (1994)*. In truth, it's likely one of the most common tropes/archetypal events in history.

I can map this onto *Batman Forever (1995)* quite easily. When he's in the circus and his parents are killed, he has left the Known, his kingdom -- his home. He left out the top to safely remove the bomb. He voluntarily entered the Unknown to help others and risk himself. Very common, basic stuff. But, when he comes back, his parents are dead -- like Sima returning to find his dead father in The Lion King. Now, his safe little world has been shattered; it's no longer the Known. Now, he has no home. Why was he punished so? Because he was arrogant and acted for his own interest and glory. This is clear with his general arrogance in the film until later on, when he actually becomes a hero and does good, not for himself. (This is clear when he tries to go out as Batman but is completely crushed by all the women out there that see right through him, that are no match for the world outside what he knows. Like Kevin stuck in New York at night, or Harry Potter down Knockturn Alley. Again: you see it time and time again.) Robin must accept, like Bruce as a child, he played a part in it. He had tricked himself, he had become lazy and soft. This is a very profound, complex idea, but runs through general morality and philosophy. It's why Ra's al Ghul tells Bruce that it's his fault that his parents were killed when he was a boy (in *Batman Begins (2005)*). Batman, like Robin, keeps finding others to blame. Keeps wanting to punish others -- like that's the right path at all.

Anyway, the death of his parents (well, his entire family, actually) symbolise his first step into heroism and his own Self in Jungian terms. For a few reasons, this is always without the parents. Either they must be left behind, or they are killed. Very common across storytelling, including the Bible, of course. I cannot even name all the movies where this sort of theme is played out, for the exact same reasons, to roughly the same conclusion (ending to the story).

It's no accident that Robin must step through a womb-like shape, as did Sima into the cave, as did Bilbo, as did Harry Potter into the Chamber of Secrets, as did Nemo and Ariel through the rocks. Or else, through a tunnel (same thing), as with real human rituals of this sort. It symbolises a cleansing, and is even used in some therapies. (Of course, you see it more broadly in sports and royal terms, when a man must run through a tunnel created by outspread arms or swords or guns.) Like Mowgil and the Snake -- primal wisdom, the positive side of the female dragon of chaos, symbolically (this concept taken from the creation myth of Babylon, by the way, dating back about 4,000 years). Like Harry Potter facing the female dragon of chaos (Basilisk) in the Chamber as to save the virgin (Ginny), like King George and the dragon, yes? Tolkien gave a spider form (Shelob) to this, yet still in her womb-like cave and, psychologically, the subconscious (hence, underground lake is also common). In the case of Sima, he sees a vision of his dead father -- of the man he could be, if he returns as king. Like Ripley at the end of *Alien (1979)* (again, a more literal female dragon of chaos, in space). Like Merlin in the TV show, seeking wisdom from the female dragon (literally a dragon this time). And, the original primal wisdom? The snake itself, of course. Miltonian and other lines of thinking frame the Snake in the Garden of Eden in this way, too. (Worth noting that this tracks, in Darwinian terms, as we know that snakes were a great predator of humans for endless years. Our eyes are literally built for snake-detection in the grass, for example. It's not unreasonable to assume that we got mental images imprinted inwardly from so many generations of this struggle -- and that we started to tell stories about the Snake as such, and its qualities. Then, in the very human way, we abstracted those out to non-snakes, including man himself; hence, 'beware the snakes in your own heart'.)

In terms of the whole, 'I am both Batman and Bruce Wayne', that's not even a question. Look at Hulk and Banner as he intergrades himself in *Endgame (2019)*, for example. Or, even the dyadic relationship between Harry Potter and Voldemort, indeed (remember: a piece of Voldemort is within Harry, literally). Luke and Vader, again. Neo and Smith. Jekyll and Hyde. Stanley Ipkiss and The Mask (his shadow form). Spider-Man and the shadow Spider-Man form. Superman and his endless shadow aspects/negative versions. So on and so forth.

Anyway, I cannot press on like this, so I'll just leave it here. I think you get my point. The fact I can list about 50 movies and stories over the years that have the same kinds of events and images and archetypes indicates something deeper and very real. Unless you believe that (a) all the artists are mindlessly copying each other; or (b) artists happened to all come t the same feelings and creations, and they are void of meaning. Both options sound positively insane and impossible, to me. 

I cannot break down every moment of Batman Forever like this, because it's not perfect, nor is it meant to be. But, I could do a decent job with most scenes and plot points. It would take two hours just to talk about the psychology of Two-Face and his 'special coin', for example.

And, I didn't even talk about the bit where Bruce actually stood up and told everybody he was Batman, but nobody heard him. And, he didn't try very hard after that, did he? There are so many layers to that, it's quite something!

It's fair to say the film expects us to give it credit for being feminist, and in particular for being feminist in a more interesting way than, for example, *Captain Marvel*, but in the end its feminism is fairly shallow. One reviewer complained about the lack of menstrual blood in the film — on the one hand, this is ridiculous, but on the other hand, they sort of had a point. A serious engagement with feminism needs to think clearly about all the (biological and social) aspects of life that make feminism a difficult and ongoing project, not just a simple matter of declaring oneself free of patriarchy. In that sense, Bella's victory comes too easily; all she needs to do is >!turn her husband into a goat, and she can live happily ever after!<. (And the film also seems to forget about >!the suffering Bella saw in Alexandria!<, which seems like another missed opportunity to deal with difficult feminist issues in an interesting way.)

Now, focusing on whether or not the film is or is not "feminist," or whether its feminism is of the good sort or the bad sort, is arguably not the most productive way to engage with the film. But it is unquestionably a form of engagement that the film invites, and once you start to think through those issues it becomes difficult to ignore them. (Complaining about the film's feminist failures is thus unlike the even more baffling online discourse about >!Bella being a "child" in the initial sex scenes!< — this is clearly not an issue that the film itself is inviting us to reflect on, but just a result of people refusing to accept the film's absurdist fairytale logic at face value.)

**Hunters in the Snow (2000)**

*A melancholic painter has an existential crisis triggered by the bulldozing of his local grocery store. There is an almost suffocating despair present throughout this movie, yet tinged with hope.*

**Tokyo Trash Baby**

*A lonely girl stalks her neighbour by collecting his trash. Low budget cinematography makes the subject matter uncomfortably voyeuristic.*

**Show Me Love (1998)**

*Two teenage girls deal with rumours about them being lesbians. Somehow avoiding ever becoming cheesy or exploitive, this movie is a sweet and charming story that fumbles along with its characters.*

**The Cement Garden**

*A teenage boy develops an unhealthy affection for his older sister. A fairly bleak look at life in the brutalist apartment blocks of England.*

**Hush! (2001)**

*An isolated and dysfunctional woman asks a gay man to be her sperm donor. All the characters in this movie are unhappy and reaching for connection, creating a series of unusual and uncomfortable situations.*

**God's Comedy**

*An eccentric ice cream maker sources his ingredients from some very strange and morally dubious places. This movie is simply bizarre and wholly unique.*

**Tamasha**

*Two people fed up with their lives cross paths on holiday, then have to deal with returning to humdrum reality. Idealistic and with some of the best montages I’ve seen. The characters have to decide whether or not to fight for their dreams or accept their mundane lives.*

**Palo Alto**

*Three teenagers struggle to find themselves in their privileged yet dysfunctional lives. Hazy and dreamlike, interwoven scenes of the lives of the characters.*

**God Help the Girl**

*A mentally ill girl finds salvation in music. A musical blending light drama with light comedy, it nevertheless has some dark moments.*

**Keiner Liebt Mich**

*A woman obsessed with death becomes close with her colourful neighbour who is full of life. The best movie to feature “La Vie en Rose” by Edith Piaf. A precious gem of a movie.*

I think your argument only works if you endorse the premise that the only purpose of film is to entertain.  Humoring this premise for a second, if entertainment is the sole purpose of a film, than of course any portrayal of suffering that gets at anything true or visceral is going to feel exploitative.  

However, I believe that film can exist outside the goal of pure entertainment to provide valuable experiences and information to audiences.  12 Years A Slave, for example, is a realistic, harrowing depiction of a historical atrocity through the eyes of the people who experienced it.  In portraying these horrors on-screen, 12 Years A Slave succeeds in inspiring empathy for the plight of enslaved people for an audience that would otherwise struggle to relate, provides historically accurate insight into the true brutality & extent of suffering that existed within the institution of slavery, and portrays a poignant story of human resilience that is emotionally impactful to audiences.  

I think it is important context to note that America in the present-day still struggles to acknowledge & properly educate about the horrors of slavery.  Where I grew up in the South, it was not uncommon for teachers to spin tall tales about "happy slaves," and even in the present, there have been many attempts by people to codify "positive" portrayals of slavery into our textbooks and educational curricula.  In a society like this, 12 Years A Slave acts an important counter to egregiously common falsehoods about the institution of slavery itself.

For that impact alone, I'd counter that the film is not exploitative but simply historically accurate.

I think a big part of it is that film distribution changed. As a loved one recently put it, it is *insane* that a gorefest like The Substance is playing in theaters. This post immediately reminded me of Michael Weldon's wonderful books about the crazy, tiny films that used to only be shown at drive-ins, and how similar they are to films that now have multimillion dollar budgets. 

> The Psychotronic Encyclopedia of Film celebrates over 3,000 movies often treated with indifference or contempt by other movie guides. Most of them are considered exploitation films. Some of them were made with such impossibly low budgets that they have never been released through regular channels of distribution. Many are now considered classics or cult films despite unfavorable critical response or initial box office failure. Critics searching for art condemn most of these features for the very reasons that millions continue to enjoy them: violence, sex, noise, and often mindless escapism....

> Today, there are more ways to watch Psychotronic films than ever before. We're in the midst of an astounding boom in the cable television and home video industries. Movies that most people didn't bother to see in the theater turn up within months on cable. Movies that would have remained unreleased or unseen except by collectors are now available to a vast market of viewers in the comfort of their homes. The promotional hype that once lured or tricked a person into spending a few bucks to see a movie is now being used to convince him to spend $60 to buy a videocassette of a film that in many cases would have put him to sleep or sent him to the exit doors in a theater. The lack of information available about the obscure films now being watched and even purchased by millions of consumers is staggering. 

When I was young, decent films about superheroes were rare. Films that were like Dungeons & Dragons back then were so rare and precious that they still hold much more sway over me than they ought to, now that they are fairly common. But another part of this is just that so many more films are being made nowadays than in the past. The volume of weird stuff probably makes it feel like a larger percentage of the whole.
